Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 53, verse 5–18:

Allah's words: ﴿He was taught by one mighty in power﴾. This refers to Jibril (peace be upon him), who taught the Prophet (ﷺ). Ibn Qutaybah said: The root of this is from "quwa al-habl" (the strands of a rope), which are its strengths; its singular is quwwah. ﴿Dhu mirrah﴾ means possessor of strength, and the root of mirrah is twisting (fatl). The exegetes said: Among his strength was that he uprooted the cities of Lot, lifted them on his wing, and overturned them; and he cried out to Thamud, and they became motionless corpses.

Allah's words: ﴿Then he stood﴾ ﴿while he was on the higher horizon﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions.

One: Jibril stood, "while he" refers to the Prophet (ﷺ); meaning they both stood on the higher horizon when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was taken on the night journey. This is the view of al-Farra'.

The second: Jibril stood, "while he" – meaning Jibril – was on the higher horizon in his true form, because he used to take on the form of a man when he descended to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with revelation, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) loved to see him in his true form. So he stood on the eastern horizon and filled the horizon. The meaning is: Jibril stood on the higher horizon in his form. This is the view of al-Zajjaj. Mujahid said: The higher horizon is the place where the sun rises. Others said: It was only called "the higher" because it is above the side of the west on the surface of the earth, not in the air.

Allah's words: ﴿Then he drew near and descended﴾. Al-Farra' said: The meaning is "then he descended and drew near," but it is permissible to put either of the two verbs first when their meaning is one, so you say: "He has approached and come near," "He came near and approached," "He reviled and insulted," "He insulted and reviled." From this is His words: ﴿The Hour has drawn near and the moon has split﴾ [al-Qamar: 1]. The meaning – and Allah knows best – is: the moon split and the Hour drew near. Ibn Qutaybah said: The meaning is: he descended and drew near, because he descended in order to approach, and drew near by descending. Al-Zajjaj said: "Dana" means "qaraba" (drew near), and "tadalla" means he increased in nearness, and the meaning of the two words is one. Others said: The origin of tadalli is descending to a thing until one comes near to it, so it was put in place of nearness.

Concerning the one referred to by His words ﴿Then he drew near﴾ there are three opinions.

The first: that it is Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Al-Bukhari and Muslim related in the two Sahihs, from the hadith of Sharik ibn Abi Namir, from Anas ibn Malik, who said: "The Almighty, the Lord of Might, drew near, then descended, until he was at a distance of two bow-lengths or closer." Abu Salamah related from Ibn Abbas regarding "Then he drew near" (p-66) that he said: "His Lord drew near and descended." This is the choice of Muqatil, who said: "The Lord drew near to Muhammad on the night he was taken on the journey, so he was at a distance of two bow-lengths or closer." I have explained this aspect in my book "al-Mughni," and clarified that it is not as may come to mind regarding the nearness of bodies and the covering of distance, because that pertains to bodies, and Allah is exalted above that.

The second: that it is Muhammad who drew near to his Lord; this was said by Ibn Abbas and al-Qurazi.

The third: that it is Jibril. Then in the speech there are two opinions.

One: Jibril drew near after his standing on the higher horizon of the earth, so he descended to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ); this was said by al-Hasan and Qatadah. The second: Jibril drew near to his Lord, Mighty and Majestic, so he was at a distance of two bow-lengths or closer; this was said by Mujahid.

Allah's words: ﴿So he was at a distance of two bow-lengths or closer﴾. Ibn Mas'ud and Abu Razin recited: "fa-kana qada qawsayn" with a dal. Abu 'Ubaydah said: al-qab and al-qad mean measure (qadr). Ibn Faris (p-67) said: al-qab means measure. It is also said: rather, al-qab is what lies between the grip and the string-notch (siyah), and each bow has two qabs. Ibn Qutaybah said: the siyah of the bow is what is bent at its two ends.

Concerning what is meant by "the two bows" there are two opinions.

One: that it is the bow with which one shoots; this was said by Ibn Abbas, and Ibn Qutaybah chose it, saying: "the measure of two bows." Al-Kisa'i said: By "the two bows" he meant one bow.

The second: that the bow is the forearm (dhira'); so the meaning is that between them was the measure of two forearms. Ibn Qutaybah related this, and it is the view of Ibn Mas'ud, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and al-Suddi. Ibn Mas'ud said: Jibril drew near to him until he was the measure of one or two forearms.

Allah's words: ﴿or closer﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions.

One: that it means "bal" (rather), this was said by Muqatil. The second: that they were addressed in their own language; the meaning is: it was, by what you estimate, the measure of two bows or less; this is the choice of al-Zajjaj.

Allah's words: ﴿So He revealed to His servant what He revealed﴾. Concerning this there are three opinions.

One: Allah revealed to Muhammad directly, without intermediary; this is according to the one who says it occurred on the night of the Mi'raj.

The second: Jibril revealed to the Prophet (ﷺ) what Allah revealed to him; this was related by 'Ata' from Ibn Abbas.

The third: Allah [revealed] to Jibril what He revealed; this is related from 'A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her), al-Hasan, and Qatadah. (p-68)

Allah's words: ﴿The heart did not lie about what it saw﴾. Abu Ja'far, Hisham from Ibn 'Amir, and Aban from 'Asim recited: "ma kadhdhaba" with a doubled dhal; the rest recited it with a single dhal. Whoever doubles it means: his heart did not deny what his eye saw; whoever reads it lightly means: his heart did not make him imagine that he saw while he had not seen, rather the heart confirmed his seeing.

Concerning what he saw there are two opinions.

One: that he saw his Lord, Mighty and Majestic; this was said by Ibn Abbas, [Anas] and al-Hasan, and Ikrimah.

The second: that he saw Jibril in his form in which he was created; this was said by Ibn Mas'ud and 'A'ishah.

Allah's words: ﴿Will you then dispute with him over what he saw?﴾ Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, al-Mufaddal, Khalaf, and Ya'qub recited: "afatumrunahu". Ibn Qutaybah said: the meaning of "afatumarunahu" is "will you dispute with him," from al-mira' (disputation), and the meaning of "afatumrunahu" is "will you deny him."

Allah's words: ﴿And he certainly saw Him in another descent﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: That is, he saw him one other time. Ibn Abbas said: Muhammad saw his Lord; the explanation of this is that he returned many times for the prayers, and saw his Lord on some of those occasions another time. Ka'b said: Allah, Exalted, divided His speech and His seeing between Muhammad and Musa: Muhammad saw Him twice, and Musa spoke with Him twice. (p-69) It is also related from Ibn Mas'ud that this sight was of Jibril too; he saw him in his form in which he was created.

As for Sidrat al-Muntaha, the sidrah is the lote tree (sidr), and it is authentically related in a hadith from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he said: "Its fruit is like the jars of Hajar, and its leaves are like the ears of elephants." Concerning its place there are two opinions.

One: that it is above the seventh heaven; this is mentioned in the two Sahihs from the hadith of Malik ibn Sa'sa'ah. Muqatil said: It is to the right of the Throne.

The second: that it is in the sixth heaven; Muslim related it in his Afrad from Ibn Mas'ud, and al-Dahhak said likewise. The exegetes said: It was called Sidrat al-Muntaha because the end of what is ascended with from the earth is to it, and it is taken from there; and to it ends what is descended with from above it, and it is taken from there; and to it ends the knowledge of all the angels.

Allah's words: ﴿near it﴾. Mu'adh al-Qari', Ibn Ya'mar, and Abu Nuhayk recited: "'indahu" with a raised ha as a masculine pronoun. ﴿The Garden of Refuge﴾. Ibn Abbas said: It is a garden to which Jibril and the angels resort. al-Hasan said: It is the one to which the people of Paradise will go. Muqatil said: It is a garden to which the spirits of martyrs resort. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, al-Sha'bi, Abu al-Mutawakkil, Abu al-Jawza', and Abu al-'Aliyah recited: "jannahu al-ma'wa" with a sound raised ha (p-70). Tha'lab said: They mean "ajannahu" (the garden that shelters it), and it is an anomalous reading. It was also said: The meaning of "'indaha" is: the night overtook him, meaning the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

Allah's words: ﴿When there covered the lote tree that which covered it﴾. Muslim related in his Afrad from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud, who said: A golden moth covered it. In the hadith of Malik ibn Sa'sa'ah from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), he said: "When there covered it from the command of Allah what covered it, it changed, so no one of Allah's creation is able to describe its beauty." al-Hasan and Muqatil said: The angels covered it like ravens when they settle on a tree. al-Dahhak said: The light of the Lord of the worlds covered it.

Allah's words: ﴿His sight did not swerve, nor did it transgress﴾. That is: the sight of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not turn right or left; ﴿nor did it transgress﴾, that is: it did not exceed or go beyond what it saw. This describes his courtesy (ﷺ) in that station.

﴿He certainly saw of the greatest signs of his Lord﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions: One: [Indeed] he saw of the great signs of his Lord. The second: Indeed he saw of the greatest [sign] of his Lord's signs.

Concerning what he saw of the signs, the exegetes have three opinions.

One: that he saw a green canopy (rafraf) from Paradise which filled the horizon; this was said by Ibn Mas'ud.

The second: that he saw Jibril in his form in which he appears in the heavens; this was said by Ibn Zayd.

The third: that he saw among the great signs and proofs of his Lord [the great signs and proofs]; this was said by Ibn Jarir.

Al-Zajjaj said: "Dana" means "qaraba" (drew near), and "tadalla" means he increased in nearness, and the meaning of the two words is one. Others said: The origin of tadalli is descending to a thing until one comes near to it, so it was put in place of nearness.

The first: that it is Allah, Mighty and Majestic. The second: Jibril drew near to his Lord, Mighty and Majestic, so he was at a distance of two bow-lengths or closer; this was said by Mujahid.

Ibn Qutaybah said: the siyah of the bow is what is bent at its two ends.

The third: that he saw among the great signs and proofs of his Lord [the great signs and proofs]; this was said by Ibn Jarir.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 53, verse 5–18:

Allah's words: ﴿He was taught by one mighty in power﴾. This refers to Jibril (peace be upon him), who taught the Prophet (ﷺ). Ibn Qutaybah said: The root of this is from "quwa al-habl" (the strands of a rope), which are its strengths; its singular is quwwah. ﴿Dhu mirrah﴾ means possessor of strength, and the root of mirrah is twisting (fatl). The exegetes said: Among his strength was that he uprooted the cities of Lot, lifted them on his wing, and overturned them; and he cried out to Thamud, and they became motionless corpses.

Allah's words: ﴿Then he stood﴾ ﴿while he was on the higher horizon﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions.

One: Jibril stood, "while he" refers to the Prophet (ﷺ); meaning they both stood on the higher horizon when the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was taken on the night journey. This is the view of al-Farra'.

The second: Jibril stood, "while he" – meaning Jibril – was on the higher horizon in his true form, because he used to take on the form of a man when he descended to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with revelation, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) loved to see him in his true form. So he stood on the eastern horizon and filled the horizon. The meaning is: Jibril stood on the higher horizon in his form. This is the view of al-Zajjaj. Mujahid said: The higher horizon is the place where the sun rises. Others said: It was only called "the higher" because it is above the side of the west on the surface of the earth, not in the air.

Allah's words: ﴿Then he drew near and descended﴾. Al-Farra' said: The meaning is "then he descended and drew near," but it is permissible to put either of the two verbs first when their meaning is one, so you say: "He has approached and come near," "He came near and approached," "He reviled and insulted," "He insulted and reviled." From this is His words: ﴿The Hour has drawn near and the moon has split﴾ [al-Qamar: 1]. The meaning – and Allah knows best – is: the moon split and the Hour drew near. Ibn Qutaybah said: The meaning is: he descended and drew near, because he descended in order to approach, and drew near by descending. Al-Zajjaj said: "Dana" means "qaraba" (drew near), and "tadalla" means he increased in nearness, and the meaning of the two words is one. Others said: The origin of tadalli is descending to a thing until one comes near to it, so it was put in place of nearness.

Concerning the one referred to by His words ﴿Then he drew near﴾ there are three opinions.

The first: that it is Allah, Mighty and Majestic. Al-Bukhari and Muslim related in the two Sahihs, from the hadith of Sharik ibn Abi Namir, from Anas ibn Malik, who said: "The Almighty, the Lord of Might, drew near, then descended, until he was at a distance of two bow-lengths or closer." Abu Salamah related from Ibn Abbas regarding "Then he drew near" (p-66) that he said: "His Lord drew near and descended." This is the choice of Muqatil, who said: "The Lord drew near to Muhammad on the night he was taken on the journey, so he was at a distance of two bow-lengths or closer." I have explained this aspect in my book "al-Mughni," and clarified that it is not as may come to mind regarding the nearness of bodies and the covering of distance, because that pertains to bodies, and Allah is exalted above that.

The second: that it is Muhammad who drew near to his Lord; this was said by Ibn Abbas and al-Qurazi.

The third: that it is Jibril. Then in the speech there are two opinions.

One: Jibril drew near after his standing on the higher horizon of the earth, so he descended to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ); this was said by al-Hasan and Qatadah. The second: Jibril drew near to his Lord, Mighty and Majestic, so he was at a distance of two bow-lengths or closer; this was said by Mujahid.

Allah's words: ﴿So he was at a distance of two bow-lengths or closer﴾. Ibn Mas'ud and Abu Razin recited: "fa-kana qada qawsayn" with a dal. Abu 'Ubaydah said: al-qab and al-qad mean measure (qadr). Ibn Faris (p-67) said: al-qab means measure. It is also said: rather, al-qab is what lies between the grip and the string-notch (siyah), and each bow has two qabs. Ibn Qutaybah said: the siyah of the bow is what is bent at its two ends.

Concerning what is meant by "the two bows" there are two opinions.

One: that it is the bow with which one shoots; this was said by Ibn Abbas, and Ibn Qutaybah chose it, saying: "the measure of two bows." Al-Kisa'i said: By "the two bows" he meant one bow.

The second: that the bow is the forearm (dhira'); so the meaning is that between them was the measure of two forearms. Ibn Qutaybah related this, and it is the view of Ibn Mas'ud, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and al-Suddi. Ibn Mas'ud said: Jibril drew near to him until he was the measure of one or two forearms.

Allah's words: ﴿or closer﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions.

One: that it means "bal" (rather), this was said by Muqatil. The second: that they were addressed in their own language; the meaning is: it was, by what you estimate, the measure of two bows or less; this is the choice of al-Zajjaj.

Allah's words: ﴿So He revealed to His servant what He revealed﴾. Concerning this there are three opinions.

One: Allah revealed to Muhammad directly, without intermediary; this is according to the one who says it occurred on the night of the Mi'raj.

The second: Jibril revealed to the Prophet (ﷺ) what Allah revealed to him; this was related by 'Ata' from Ibn Abbas.

The third: Allah [revealed] to Jibril what He revealed; this is related from 'A'ishah (may Allah be pleased with her), al-Hasan, and Qatadah. (p-68)

Allah's words: ﴿The heart did not lie about what it saw﴾. Abu Ja'far, Hisham from Ibn 'Amir, and Aban from 'Asim recited: "ma kadhdhaba" with a doubled dhal; the rest recited it with a single dhal. Whoever doubles it means: his heart did not deny what his eye saw; whoever reads it lightly means: his heart did not make him imagine that he saw while he had not seen, rather the heart confirmed his seeing.

Concerning what he saw there are two opinions.

One: that he saw his Lord, Mighty and Majestic; this was said by Ibn Abbas, [Anas] and al-Hasan, and Ikrimah.

The second: that he saw Jibril in his form in which he was created; this was said by Ibn Mas'ud and 'A'ishah.

Allah's words: ﴿Will you then dispute with him over what he saw?﴾ Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, al-Mufaddal, Khalaf, and Ya'qub recited: "afatumrunahu". Ibn Qutaybah said: the meaning of "afatumarunahu" is "will you dispute with him," from al-mira' (disputation), and the meaning of "afatumrunahu" is "will you deny him."

Allah's words: ﴿And he certainly saw Him in another descent﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: That is, he saw him one other time. Ibn Abbas said: Muhammad saw his Lord; the explanation of this is that he returned many times for the prayers, and saw his Lord on some of those occasions another time. Ka'b said: Allah, Exalted, divided His speech and His seeing between Muhammad and Musa: Muhammad saw Him twice, and Musa spoke with Him twice. (p-69) It is also related from Ibn Mas'ud that this sight was of Jibril too; he saw him in his form in which he was created.

As for Sidrat al-Muntaha, the sidrah is the lote tree (sidr), and it is authentically related in a hadith from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) that he said: "Its fruit is like the jars of Hajar, and its leaves are like the ears of elephants." Concerning its place there are two opinions.

One: that it is above the seventh heaven; this is mentioned in the two Sahihs from the hadith of Malik ibn Sa'sa'ah. Muqatil said: It is to the right of the Throne.

The second: that it is in the sixth heaven; Muslim related it in his Afrad from Ibn Mas'ud, and al-Dahhak said likewise. The exegetes said: It was called Sidrat al-Muntaha because the end of what is ascended with from the earth is to it, and it is taken from there; and to it ends what is descended with from above it, and it is taken from there; and to it ends the knowledge of all the angels.

Allah's words: ﴿near it﴾. Mu'adh al-Qari', Ibn Ya'mar, and Abu Nuhayk recited: "'indahu" with a raised ha as a masculine pronoun. ﴿The Garden of Refuge﴾. Ibn Abbas said: It is a garden to which Jibril and the angels resort. al-Hasan said: It is the one to which the people of Paradise will go. Muqatil said: It is a garden to which the spirits of martyrs resort. Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab, al-Sha'bi, Abu al-Mutawakkil, Abu al-Jawza', and Abu al-'Aliyah recited: "jannahu al-ma'wa" with a sound raised ha (p-70). Tha'lab said: They mean "ajannahu" (the garden that shelters it), and it is an anomalous reading. It was also said: The meaning of "'indaha" is: the night overtook him, meaning the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

Allah's words: ﴿When there covered the lote tree that which covered it﴾. Muslim related in his Afrad from the hadith of Ibn Mas'ud, who said: A golden moth covered it. In the hadith of Malik ibn Sa'sa'ah from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), he said: "When there covered it from the command of Allah what covered it, it changed, so no one of Allah's creation is able to describe its beauty." al-Hasan and Muqatil said: The angels covered it like ravens when they settle on a tree. al-Dahhak said: The light of the Lord of the worlds covered it.

Allah's words: ﴿His sight did not swerve, nor did it transgress﴾. That is: the sight of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) did not turn right or left; ﴿nor did it transgress﴾, that is: it did not exceed or go beyond what it saw. This describes his courtesy (ﷺ) in that station.

﴿He certainly saw of the greatest signs of his Lord﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions: One: [Indeed] he saw of the great signs of his Lord. The second: Indeed he saw of the greatest [sign] of his Lord's signs.

Concerning what he saw of the signs, the exegetes have three opinions.

One: that he saw a green canopy (rafraf) from Paradise which filled the horizon; this was said by Ibn Mas'ud.

The second: that he saw Jibril in his form in which he appears in the heavens; this was said by Ibn Zayd.

The third: that he saw among the great signs and proofs of his Lord [the great signs and proofs]; this was said by Ibn Jarir.

Al-Zajjaj said: When Allah the Exalted had related these narratives, He said: ﴿Have you considered al-Lat and al-'Uzza?﴾ The meaning is: Tell us about these deities you worship. Do they possess any of the power and greatness with which the Lord of Might is described?

As for "al-Lat" (اللّاتُ), the majority of readers pronounce the ta' lightly. It was the name of an idol belonging to the tribe of Thaqif, which they took as a deity besides Allah. They would derive names for their idols from the names of Allah the Exalted: from "Allah" they formed "al-Lat," and from "al-'Aziz" (the Mighty) they formed "al-'Uzza." Abu Sulayman al-Khattabi said: The polytheists used the name "Allah" as a name for some of their idols, so Allah turned it toward al-Lat to safeguard this name and defend it.

Ibn Abbas, Abu Razin, Abu 'Abd al-Rahman al-Sulami, al-Dahhak, Ibn al-Sumayfa', Mujahid, Ibn Ya'mar, al-A'mash, and Warsh from Ya'qub read "al-Lattu" (اللّاتَّ) with a doubled ta'. It is reported in the explanation of this reading from Ibn Abbas and Mujahid that a man used to knead sawiq (a parched grain porridge) for the pilgrims. When he died, they devoted themselves to his grave and worshipped him. Al-Zajjaj said: They claimed that a man used to knead sawiq and sell it beside that idol, so the idol was named "al-Lattu" (اللّاتَّ). Al-Kisa'i would stop on it with a haa', saying "al-Lah" (اللّاهْ). This is an analogical reading, but the better practice is to stop with a ta', following the mushaf (the written Qur'an).

As for "al-'Uzza," there are two views.

The first: it was a tree belonging to Ghatafan, which they worshipped. This was said by Mujahid.

The second: it was an idol belonging to them. This was said by al-Dahhak. He said: As for "Manat," it was an idol of Hudhayl and Khuza'ah, which the people of Makkah worshipped. Qatadah said: Rather, it belonged to the Ansar. Abu 'Ubaydah said: Al-Lat, al-'Uzza, and Manat were idols of stone inside the Ka'bah, which they worshipped. Ibn Kathir read "wa-Muna'ah" (وَمُناءَةَ) with a long vowel and a hamza.

As for His saying "al-thalitha" (الثّالِثَةَ), it is an attribute of "Manat." It is the third of the two idols in mention. "Al-ukhra" (الأُخْرى) is also an attribute of it. Al-Tha'labi said: The Arabs do not say "al-ukhra" for the third; rather, "al-ukhra" is an attribute of the second. So there are two explanations of the meaning.

The first: this is for the sake of matching the endings of the verses (ra'su al-ayi, the rhyme of the verse-endings), as in His saying ﴿other uses (مَآرِبُ أُخْرى)﴾ [Ta-Ha: 18], where He did not say "ukhar." This was said by al-Khalil.

The second: there is inversion in the verse, and its sense is: "Have you considered al-Lat and al-'Uzza, the other (al-ukhra), and Manat, the third (al-thalitha)?" This was said by al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl.

His saying the Exalted: ﴿Is the male for you?﴾ Ibn al-Sa'ib said: The polytheists of Quraysh said of the idols and the angels: "They are the daughters of Allah." When one of them was given the good news of a female child, he would be displeased. So Allah the Exalted said, rebuking them: ﴿Is the male for you and the female for Him?﴾ He means the idols, which are feminine in their names.

﴿That, then, is an unjust division.﴾ Asim, Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i read "dizaa" (ضِيزى) with a kasrah on the dad without a hamza. Ibn Kathir agreed with them on the kasrah but added a hamza. Ubayy ibn Ka'b and Mu'adh al-Qari read "daizaa" (ضَيْزى) with a fathah on the dad without a hamza. Al-Zajjaj said: In the Arabic language, "al-dizaa" means deficient and unjust. It is said: "daazahu yadiuhu" when he diminished his right. It is also said: "da'aza yad'azuhu" with a hamza. The grammarians agreed that the original form of "dizaa" is "duzaa." Their argument is that it was transposed from the pattern "fu'la" as "duzaa" to "dizaa," so that the yaa' would be preserved, as they said "abyad" and "biid" (white and whites), whose original was "buud," and the dammah was changed to a kasrah. I read to some scholars of the language: there are several forms for "dizaa": it is said "dizaa," "duzaa," "du'zaa," and "da'zaa" with a fathah on the pattern "fa'laa." In the Qur'an, only "dizaa" with a yaa' that is not hamzated is permissible. The grammarians did not say that it retains its original form, because they do not know of "fi'la" as an adjective in speech. They know adjectives on the pattern "fa'la" with a fathah, such as "sakra" and "ghadba," or with a dammah, such as "hubla" and "fudla."

His saying the Exalted: ﴿They are only names﴾, meaning the idols, ﴿which you and your fathers have named, for which Allah has sent down no authority﴾. The meaning is: These idols, which they named with these appellations, have no reality beneath them, for they neither harm nor benefit. They are mere labels placed upon inanimate things. ﴿Allah has not sent down any authority concerning them﴾, that is, He has not sent down a book containing evidence for what they claim, that these are gods. Then He turned from addressing them to speaking about them, saying: ﴿They follow only conjecture and what their souls desire﴾ concerning their being gods, meaning what Satan had adorned for them. ﴿And there has certainly come to them from their Lord guidance﴾, meaning clarification through the Book and the Messenger. Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 53, verse 27–30:

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, those who do not believe in the Hereafter﴾ — that is, in the Resurrection — ﴿name the angels with names of females﴾, and that is when they claimed that they are the daughters of Allah. ﴿And they have no knowledge of it﴾ — that is, they do not have certainty that they are females. ﴿They follow not except assumption, and indeed, assumption avails not against the truth at all﴾ — that is, it does not stand in place of knowledge; so "the truth" here means knowledge.

﴿So turn away from one who turns away from Our remembrance﴾ — meaning the Qur'an. According to the exegetes, this is abrogated (mansukh) by the verse of the sword.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿That is the extent of their knowledge﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: They only know what they need for their livelihood, and they have cast aside the matter of the Hereafter.

His saying, exalted is He, ﴿He is most knowing of who has strayed from His way...﴾ — the verse; and the meaning is that He is Knowing of both groups, so He will recompense them.

Allah says: ﴿And to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth.﴾ This is an informing about His power and the vastness of His dominion. It is a parenthetical statement placed between the first verse and His saying: ﴿that He may recompense those who did evil with what they have done﴾, because the lam in "liyajziya" (so that He may recompense) is connected to the meaning of the first verse. That is, when He knows both of them, He recompenses each according to what it deserves. This is the lam of consequence (lam al-'aqibah), since His knowledge of the two groups led to their being recompensed according to what they merit. He is only able to recompense both groups if His dominion is vast, so He informed of it in His saying: ﴿And to Allah belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth.﴾

The exegetes said: "wa-asa'u" (and those who did evil) means "those who associated partners with Allah," and "wa-ahsanu" (and those who did good) means "those who affirmed His oneness (tawhid)." Al-husna (the best) is Paradise. The major sins are mentioned in Surah al-Nisa' (4:31). It was said: the "major sins of wrongdoing" (kaba'ir al-ithm) are every sin that is concluded with the Fire, and the "shameful deeds" (al-fawahish) are every sin for which there is a prescribed punishment (hadd).

Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, al-Mufaddal and Khalaf read: "yajtanibuna kabira al-ithm" (they avoid the major sin). Al-lamam (the minor lapses) in the speech of the Arabs means approaching something. There are six sayings regarding its meaning here:

The first: what they committed of sin and shameful deeds in the Jahiliyyah, for it is forgiven in Islam. This was said by Zayd ibn Thabit.

The second: that a person commits a sin once and then repents and does not return to it. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, and al-Suddi.

The third: that it refers to minor sins, such as a glance and a kiss, and whatever falls short of fornication. This was said by Ibn Mas'ud, Abu Hurayrah, al-Sha'bi, and Masruq. This is supported by the hadith of Abu Hurayrah from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), who said: "Allah has written for the son of Adam his share of fornication. The fornication of the eyes is the gaze, the fornication of the tongue is speech, the soul desires and wishes, and the private part confirms that or denies it. If the private part advances, it is fornication; otherwise it is lamam."

The fourth: that it is what a person intends (yahimm bihi). This was said by Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah.

The fifth: that it is what occurs to the heart, i.e., passes through it. This was said by Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab.

The sixth: that it is a glance without deliberate intent. This was said by al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl. According to the first two sayings, the exception (al-istithna') is from the same genus; according to the remaining sayings, it is not from the same genus.

Allah says: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is vast in forgiveness.﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: this is for one who does that and then repents. Here the speech is complete. It was said: the "major sins of wrongdoing" (kaba'ir al-ithm) are every sin that is concluded with the Fire, and the "shameful deeds" (al-fawahish) are every sin for which there is a prescribed punishment (hadd).

The fourth: that it is what a person intends (yahimm bihi). This was said by Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah.

The fifth: that it is what occurs to the heart, i.e., passes through it. This was said by Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab.

The commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 53, verses 33–41:

Regarding His words, ﴿Have you seen the one who turned away?﴾, the scholars differed about who it was revealed concerning, giving four opinions.

The first is that it was al-Walid ibn al-Mughira. He had followed the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in his religion, but some of the polytheists reproached him and said, "You have abandoned the religion of our elders and misled them?" He said, "I feared the punishment of Allah." So they guaranteed him that if he gave them some of his wealth and returned to his polytheism, they would bear the punishment of Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, on his behalf. He did so, gave them part of what he had promised, then became stingy and withheld the rest. So this verse was revealed. This was said by Mujahid and Ibn Zayd.

The second is that it was al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, who gave five she-camels to a poor Muslim until he apostatized from his Islam, and [al-Nadr] guaranteed that he would bear his sin. This was said by al-Dahhak.

The third is that it was Abu Jahl, because he said, "By Allah, Muhammad only commands us to noble character." This was said by Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi.

The fourth is that it was al-As ibn Wa'il al-Sahmi, who sometimes agreed with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in some matters. This was said by al-Suddi.

The meaning of "turned away" (tawalla) is that he turned away from faith. ﴿And gave little﴾: concerning this there are four opinions.

The first is that he obeyed a little and then disobeyed. This was said by Ibn Abbas. The second is that he gave a little of himself by listening, then stopped short by breaking off. This was said by Mujahid. The third is that he gave a little of his wealth and then withheld it. This was said by al-Dahhak. The fourth is that he gave a little of good with his tongue and then ceased. This was said by Muqatil. Ibn Qutaybah said: the meaning of "akda" is "cut off." It derives from the *kudyat al-rakiyya*, which is the hardness in a well. When the digger reaches it, he despairs of digging further and stops the digging. Thus it is said of anyone who seeks something but does not reach its end, or who gives but does not complete it: "akda."

Regarding His words, ﴿Has he knowledge of the unseen so that he sees?﴾, there are two opinions.

One is: "so that he sees his state in the Hereafter." This was said by al-Farra'. The second is: "so that he knows what is hidden from him of the affairs of the Hereafter and other matters." This was said by Ibn Qutaybah.

Regarding His words, ﴿Or has he not been informed of what is in the scrolls of Musa,﴾ meaning the Torah, ﴿and Ibrahim﴾, meaning and the scrolls of Ibrahim. In the hadith of Abu Dharr from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Allah, the Exalted, sent down to Ibrahim ten scrolls, and He sent down to Musa, before the Torah, ten scrolls."

(p-79)

Regarding His words, ﴿who fulfilled﴾: Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Abu Imran al-Jawni, and Ibn al-Sumayfa' al-Yamani read *wafa* (وَفى) with a light *fa*. Al-Zajjaj said: *waffa* (وَفّى) is more emphatic than *wafa* (وَفى), because what he was tested with was among the greatest trials. The exegetes gave ten opinions regarding "who fulfilled."

The first is that he completed his day's work with four rak'ahs at the beginning of the day. Abu Umama narrated this from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

The second is that he fulfilled [it] with words he used to say. Sahl ibn Mu'adh ibn Anas al-Juhani narrated from his father, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "Shall I not inform you why Allah named Ibrahim His friend, [the one who fulfilled]? Because he used to say whenever he woke in the morning and whenever he entered the evening: ﴿So glory be to Allah when you enter the evening and when you enter the morning…﴾ [al-Rum: 17], and he finished the verse."

(p-80)

The third is that he fulfilled obedience in what he did with his son. al-Awfi narrated this from Ibn Abbas, and al-Qurazi also said it.

The fourth is that he fulfilled to his Lord all the laws of Islam. Ikrimah narrated this meaning from Ibn Abbas.

The fifth is that he fulfilled what he was commanded to convey of the message. This was also narrated from Ibn Abbas.

The sixth is that he acted upon what he was commanded. This was said by al-Hasan, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and Qatadah. Mujahid said: he fulfilled what was obligated upon him.

The seventh is that he fulfilled the conveying of these verses, which are: ﴿that no bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another﴾ and what follows. This is narrated from Ikrimah, Mujahid, and al-Nakha'i.

The eighth is that he fulfilled the matter of the rites. This was said by al-Dahhak.

The ninth is that he vowed not to ask any created being for anything. When he was thrown into the fire, Jibril said to him, "Do you have a need?" He said, "As for you, no." So he fulfilled what he had vowed. Ata' ibn al-Sa'ib mentioned this.

The tenth is that he discharged the trust. This was said by Sufyan ibn Uyayna.

Then He explained what is in their two scrolls, saying: ﴿that no bearer of burdens will bear the burden of another﴾, meaning: no soul carrying a load will carry the load of another. The meaning is: one will not be taken to account for the sin of another.

Its meaning is: man has nothing except the reward of his striving; if he does good, he is rewarded with good, and if he does evil, he is repaid with evil. The scholars differed concerning this verse, giving eight opinions.

(p-81)

The first is that it is abrogated (naskh, meaning abrogated or superseded) by His words: ﴿And We will join them to their descendants in faith﴾ [al-Tur: 21], so the children enter Paradise due to the righteousness of their parents. This was said by Ibn Abbas, but it is not sound, because the wording of both verses is in the form of information, and reports are not abrogated.

The second is that this applied to the people of Ibrahim and Musa, but as for this nation, they have what they strive for and what others strive for on their behalf. This was said by Ikrimah, who cited the Prophet's (ﷺ) words to the woman who asked him: "My father died without performing Hajj." He said, "Perform Hajj on his behalf."

The third is that the word "man" (insan) here refers to the disbeliever. As for the believer, he has what he strives for and what is strived for on his behalf. This was said by al-Rabi' ibn Anas.

The fourth is that man has nothing except what he strives for by way of justice. As for by way of grace, it is permissible that Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, increases for him whatever He wills. This was said by al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl.

The fifth is that the meaning of "what he strove for" is what he intended. This was said by Abu Bakr al-Warraq.

The seventh is that the lam (ل) here means "upon" (على), so the meaning is: nothing is upon man except what he strives for.

One is: "it will be known." This was said by Ibn Qutaybah.

The second is: "the servant will see his striving on the Day of Resurrection," meaning he will see his deed in his scale. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

Regarding His words, ﴿then he will be recompensed for it with the fullest recompense﴾: the pronoun "hu" refers to the striving, ﴿the fullest recompense﴾, meaning the most complete and perfect.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 53, verses 42–55:**

﴿And that to your Lord is the final return﴾, meaning the final destination of the servants and their return. Al-Zajjaj said: "All of this is in the scriptures of Ibrahim and Musa."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And that it is He who makes laugh and makes weep﴾. ʿĀʾisha said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ passed by a people who were laughing, and he said: 'If you knew what I know, you would laugh little and weep much.' Then Jibril (peace be upon him) descended with this verse. He returned to them and said: (p-83) 'I had not taken forty steps before Jibril came to me and said: Go to these people and tell them that Allah says: And that it is He who makes laugh and makes weep.'" In this there is a warning that all actions are by the decree and predestination of Allah, including laughing and weeping. Mujahid said: "He makes the people of Paradise laugh and the people of Hellfire weep." Al-Dahhak said: "He makes the earth laugh with vegetation and makes the sky weep with rain."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And that it is He who causes death﴾ in this world ﴿and gives life﴾ for the resurrection (al-baʿth).

﴿And that He created the pairs﴾, meaning the two kinds, ﴿the male and the female﴾ from all animals, ﴿from a drop of semen when it is emitted﴾. Regarding this there are two opinions.

One: when it is poured into the womb. This was said by Ibn al-Sāʾib.

The second: when it is shaped and measured. ﴿And that upon Him is the second creation﴾, which is the second creation for the resurrection on the Day of Judgment.

﴿And that it is He who enriches﴾. Regarding this there are four opinions.

One: He enriches with sufficiency. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas. The second: with livelihood. This was said by al-Dahhak. The third: with wealth. This was said by Abu Salih. The fourth: with contentment. This was said by Sufyan.

Regarding His saying ﴿aqnā﴾ there are three opinions:

One: He makes one content with what He has given. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: He gives servants (for) service (akhdama). This was said by al-Hasan and Qatada. And from Mujahid it is like the two opinions.

The third: He made for a person a possession (qinya), which is the origin of wealth. This was said by Abu ʿUbayda.

(p-84) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And that it is He who is the Lord of al-Shiʿrā﴾. Ibn Qutayba said: it is the star that rises after al-Jawzāʾ, and some of the Arabs used to worship it.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And that He destroyed ʿĀd the first﴾. Ibn Kathir, ʿĀṣim, Ibn ʿĀmir, Hamza and al-Kisāʾī recited "ʿĀdan al-ūlā" with tanwīn (ʿādan al-ūlā). Nāfiʿ and Abu ʿAmr recited "ʿādan lūlā" with the hamza dropped and the lām joined and assimilated (muwassala mudghama). Then regarding them there are two opinions.

One: they are the people of Hud, and they had a later generation, so they became ʿĀd the later (al-ukhrā). This is the view of the majority.

The second: the people of Hud are ʿĀd the later, and they are from the descendants of ʿĀd the first. This was said by Kaʿb al-Ahbar. Al-Zajjaj said: Regarding "al-ūlā" there are dialects. The best of them is the lām being sukūn with the hamza retained. The next in excellence is the lām with ḍamma and the hamza dropped. Among the Arabs there are those who say "lūlā," meaning "al-ūlā," so the hamza is dropped because the lām is vowelled.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the people of Nuh before, indeed they were more unjust and more transgressing﴾, meaning before ʿĀd and Thamud, ﴿than others,﴾ because of the long duration of Nuh's call to them and their obstinacy.

﴿And the overturned cities﴾, the towns of the people of Lut, ﴿He hurled down﴾ [meaning]: He brought them down. The one who carried this out was Jibril after He had raised them up, and Allah followed them with stones. That is His saying: ﴿Then He covered them with what covered﴾, meaning He clothed them with what clothed them, namely the stones. ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you dispute?﴾ This is an address to humankind. When Allah enumerated what He had done, which points to His oneness, He said: "Which of the blessings of your Lord, which point to His oneness, will you doubt?" Ibn ʿAbbas said: "Which of the favours of your Lord will you deny, O Walid," meaning [al-Walid] ibn al-Mughira.

﴿And the overturned cities﴾, the towns of the people of Lut, ﴿He hurled down﴾ [meaning]: He brought them down. The one who carried this out was Jibril after He had raised them up, and Allah followed them with stones. That is His saying: ﴿Then He covered them with what covered﴾, meaning He clothed them with what clothed them, namely the stones. ﴿So which of the favours of your Lord will you dispute?﴾ This is an address to humankind. When Allah enumerated what He had done, which points to His oneness, He said: "Which of the blessings of your Lord, which point to His oneness, will you doubt?" Ibn ʿAbbas said: "Which of the favours of your Lord will you deny, O Walid," meaning [al-Walid] ibn al-Mughira.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 53, verses 42–55:**

﴿And that to your Lord is the final return﴾, meaning the final destination of the servants and their return. Al-Zajjaj said: "All of this is in the scriptures of Ibrahim and Musa."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And that it is He who makes laugh and makes weep﴾. ʿĀʾisha said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ passed by a people who were laughing, and he said: 'If you knew what I know, you would laugh little and weep much.' Then Jibril (peace be upon him) descended with this verse. He returned to them and said: (p-83) 'I had not taken forty steps before Jibril came to me and said: Go to these people and tell them that Allah says: And that it is He who makes laugh and makes weep.'" In this there is a warning that all actions are by the decree and predestination of Allah, including laughing and weeping. Mujahid said: "He makes the people of Paradise laugh and the people of Hellfire weep." Al-Dahhak said: "He makes the earth laugh with vegetation and makes the sky weep with rain."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And that it is He who causes death﴾ in this world ﴿and gives life﴾ for the resurrection (al-baʿth).

﴿And that He created the pairs﴾, meaning the two kinds, ﴿the male and the female﴾ from all animals, ﴿from a drop of semen when it is emitted﴾. Regarding this there are two opinions.

One: when it is poured into the womb. This was said by Ibn al-Sāʾib.

The second: when it is shaped and measured. ﴿And that upon Him is the second creation﴾, which is the second creation for the resurrection on the Day of Judgment.

﴿And that it is He who enriches﴾. Regarding this there are four opinions.

One: He enriches with sufficiency. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas. The second: with livelihood. This was said by al-Dahhak. The third: with wealth. This was said by Abu Salih. The fourth: with contentment. This was said by Sufyan.

Regarding His saying ﴿aqnā﴾ there are three opinions:

One: He makes one content with what He has given. This was said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: He gives servants (for) service (akhdama). This was said by al-Hasan and Qatada. And from Mujahid it is like the two opinions.

The third: He made for a person a possession (qinya), which is the origin of wealth. This was said by Abu ʿUbayda.

(p-84) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And that it is He who is the Lord of al-Shiʿrā﴾. Ibn Qutayba said: it is the star that rises after al-Jawzāʾ, and some of the Arabs used to worship it.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And that He destroyed ʿĀd the first﴾. Ibn Kathir, ʿĀṣim, Ibn ʿĀmir, Hamza and al-Kisāʾī recited "ʿĀdan al-ūlā" with tanwīn (ʿādan al-ūlā). Nāfiʿ and Abu ʿAmr recited "ʿādan lūlā" with the hamza dropped and the lām joined and assimilated (muwassala mudghama). Then regarding them there are two opinions.

One: they are the people of Hud, and they had a later generation, so they became ʿĀd the later (al-ukhrā). This is the view of the majority.

The second: the people of Hud are ʿĀd the later, and they are from the descendants of ʿĀd the first. This was said by Kaʿb al-Ahbar. Al-Zajjaj said: Regarding "al-ūlā" there are dialects. The best of them is the lām being sukūn with the hamza retained. The next in excellence is the lām with ḍamma and the hamza dropped. Among the Arabs there are those who say "lūlā," meaning "al-ūlā," so the hamza is dropped because the lām is vowelled.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And the people of Nuh before, indeed they were more unjust and more transgressing﴾, meaning before ʿĀd and Thamud, ﴿than others,﴾ because of the long duration of Nuh's call to them and their obstinacy.

﴿And the overturned cities﴾, the towns of the people of Lut, ﴿He hurled down﴾ [meaning]: He brought them down. The one who carried this out was Jibril after He had raised them up, and Allah followed them with stones. Ibn ʿAbbas said: "Which of the favours of your Lord will you deny, O Walid," meaning [al-Walid] ibn al-Mughira.

(p-85) His saying, the Exalted: ﴿This is a warner﴾ — concerning it there are two opinions.

One: that it refers to the Qur'an, a warner with what the earlier Scriptures warned of. This was said by Qatadah.

The second: that it refers to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), a warner with what the Prophets warned of. This was said by Ibn Jurayj.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿The imminent one has drawn near﴾, i.e., the Resurrection has drawn near. ﴿There is none to disclose it besides Allah﴾ — concerning it there are two opinions.

One: when its hardships and terrors overwhelm creation, no one will disclose it or turn it back. This was said by ʿAtaʾ, Qatadah, and al-Ḍaḥḥāk.

The second: there is no one who can disclose its knowledge besides Allah, i.e., none knows its knowledge except Allah. This was said by al-Farrāʾ, who said: the feminine form of "kāshifah" is like His saying: ﴿Do you see any remnant of them?﴾ [al-Ḥāqqah: 8], meaning "from any remnant"; and "al-ʿāfiyah," "al-bāqiyah," and "al-nāhiyah" all carry the sense of a verbal noun. Others said: the feminine form of "kāshifah" is according to the implied phrase "a soul that discloses."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Is it at this discourse that you marvel﴾ — Muqatil said: it means the Qur'an, ﴿and laugh﴾ mockingly, ﴿and do not weep﴾ at what it contains of threat?! By this he means the disbelievers of Makkah. ﴿While you are samidun﴾ — concerning it there are five opinions. (p-86) One: heedless of play (lahw), narrated by al-ʿAwfī from Ibn ʿAbbas, and this was said by al-Farrāʾ and al-Zajjāj. Abu ʿUbayda said: it is said, "Leave off your sumud," meaning your play (lahw).

The second: turning away (muʿriḍūn), said by Mujahid.

The third: that it means singing, a Yemeni dialect; they say, "Ismud lana," meaning, "Sing for us." This was narrated by ʿIkrimah from Ibn ʿAbbas. ʿIkrimah said: it is singing in Himyaritic.

The fourth: heedless (ghafilun), said by Qatadah.

The fifth: insolent and exultant (ashirun batirun), said by al-Ḍaḥḥāk.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So prostrate to Allah﴾ — concerning it there are two opinions.

One: that it is the prostration of recitation, said by Ibn Masʿud.

The second: the obligatory prostration in the prayer.

Muqatil said: by His saying "prostrate" he means the five daily prayers.

Concerning His saying: ﴿and worship﴾ there are two opinions.

One: that it is monotheism (al-tawhid). The second: worship (al-ʿibadah).
